band.text:
The three hides are the near hide by the cottage, the middle hide at the sluice and the far hide on
the shingle spit, and each is looked after by a named volunteer who checks it weekly, sweeps it,
clears the shutters and reports anything broken. Shutters are closed at dusk by the last person out,
and a shutter left open overnight in winter has twice cost the observatory a hide floor.

The library in the cottage is a shelf of field guides, the county avifauna, forty bound years of the log
and a box of reprints, and it is for use in the cottage rather than for borrowing. A volunteer who
wants a book at home asks the recorder, who will usually say yes and write it in the loans book, and
will usually remember. The bound logs never leave the building, because they are the only copy and
the observatory has no fire safe.

The marsh itself is managed by the trust, not the observatory, and the volunteers do not cut, dig,
burn or plant anything without the trust's warden asking them to. What the observatory does do is
watch, and report: a blocked sluice, a fallen fence, a stranded seal, a fire on the shingle, an angler

provenance.key:
Sightings boards in each hide are wiped and rewritten every morning by the census walker, with
the date, the state of the tide and anything worth looking for. Visitors add to them in pencil during
the day and are asked to initial what they add. A board that still shows yesterday's date by mid-
morning is a sign that the census was not walked, and the warden will ask why, and will want an
answer.

Telescopes and binoculars in the cottage may be borrowed by visitors against a signature and a car
key, and are cleaned and put away by the volunteer on the desk at closing. The big telescope on the
cottage balcony is not lent and not moved; it is focused on the sluice for a reason, and the reason is
written on the card beside it.

School parties come in the spring and the autumn, book in advance and bring their own adults, and
are met at the car park by two volunteers who walk them in along the boardwalk with the rules
explained once, kindly, before anyone reaches the marsh. The education pack is on the shelf by the
desk with the risk assessment inside it, and both are read before the party arrives.

The cottage is open from ten to four in the season and at weekends in winter, staffed by one
volunteer at the desk and one free to walk out to a hide with a visitor who needs help. The desk
volunteer keeps the visitor book, the log and the kettle, answers the telephone, and does not leave
the desk to look at a bird unless the other volunteer has come back to cover it.

Money is taken for the guidebook, the tea and the collecting box, is counted at closing by two people
and banked weekly by the treasurer. The float is thirty pounds. The collecting box matters more
than the sales, and the total is written on the whiteboard where every volunteer can see how the
month is going.

Dogs are not allowed on the marsh at any time, on or off a lead, and the sign at the car park says so
in words and pictures. A visitor who arrives with a dog is offered the cottage balcony, which has the
best view of the sluice anyway, and most go away content. The rule is the trust's, not the
observatory's, and the volunteers do not negotiate it.

The accident book, the first-aid kit and the throw line live by the cottage door, and the throw line
goes out with anyone walking the far section in winter. The kit is checked monthly and the check
signed for on the lid. Every incident, however small, goes in the book the same day with what
happened and what was done about it.
